I, I, I wanted to understand why he did what he did, you know, they. Uh, all the, the, the crazy things he went through to try to hide his presence, to try to take advantage of his in-laws even when he wasn't in the process of trying to kill them. And at the end, he was so angry about it that he thought he'd take out his in-laws in order to be able to get some more. Um, he, he, he was *** guy who believed he deserved *** lot, and he came off that way in the prison. You know, what do you think most folks will find surprising about this particular episode? This is one of the wilder stories we've covered in *** while. I think you know, like, 11 of the producers that I worked with on this who was keeping track of it early on, would call me every few days and say, you won't believe what I've just heard. You won't believe what they're, what they're finding out. You won't believe what I just saw, um, and, and those kind of, uh, those kind of stories in our, my work are rare and, um. They're remarkable and that that that the investigation turns into something which can be very fraught from the inside or one of the investigators, but from the outside looking in, it's absolutely fascinating, uh and, and the whole process was just really interesting to watch. It's *** strange. Tragic story, as they tend to be, um. But it's, it's, it's full of depth, it's full of interesting characters with their own pasts. Each one of them has *** past. Which is fascinating. You know, I want to touch real quickly again on just having that one on one with Dan Serafini. Um. He, as you touched on, he's *** little bit of *** perplexing character, um. Did you, did you go in there with any preconceived notions of what you may have, uh, thought that he might, you know, maybe sometimes some folks are behind bars for an extended period of time and all of *** sudden they might seem *** little bit more remorseful. Yes, and I don't know if I was going in looking for remorse, uh, as much as just some kind of something that will tell me why, you know, that there was one of my favorite authors, he was *** fellow who wrote the Inspector May Gray novels as Paris detective, uh, whose motto was, I'm not here to judge, I'm here to understand, and, and I feel like that's our role. We want to just understand what the heck happened here and why did it happen, why did you do what you did. But I guess I went *** step farther than he wanted me to go because though the jury had decided he did what he did and though the evidence was Considerable against him and stacked up in *** way that couldn't be avoided, um, he wanted me to believe that he was badly done by the jury. Well that's all he really cared about saying was that I was, I was convicted for *** crime I didn't do well. You know, that it didn't look like that kind of situation to me. Yeah, and the jury agrees. Mr. Morrison, it's, it's such an honor and *** pleasure to speak with you. I really appreciate your time this morning. Delighted to be here and thank you so much. All right, thank you. 'An angry individual': Keith Morrison describes interview with Dan Serafini for ‘Dateline: Deadly Swagger’ Updated: 3:04 PM PDT Apr 17, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ NBC’s “Dateline” airs a two-hour episode on Friday focused on a Northern California crime that KCRA 3 followed closely, the murder case against former MLB pitcher Dan Serafini.Serafini was sentenced earlier this year in the June 2021 ambush-style shooting of his in-laws at their Lake Tahoe-area home. A judge denied his bid for a new trial after he claimed ineffective counsel. The convicted killer was then sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Gary Spohr died from the shooting. Wood survived and made a full recovery, but she later killed herself.During sentencing, Serafini maintained that he wasn’t a killer and decried the justice system.“Dateline’s” Keith Morrison secured a jailhouse interview with Serafini.Asked how he came across, Morrison said that Serafini threatened to walk out early on during the interview because he didn’t like the challenging questions he was asked. “I hate to even portray somebody this way, but he was an angry individual,” Morrison said. “I guess he’s angry that he was convicted and didn’t believe that he should have been.”Morrison noted that the prosecutor in the case talked about a “certain arrogance” from Serafini and “that was certainly on display.”Morrison said he wanted to understand why he did what he did. “He was a guy who believed he deserved a lot and he came off that way,” he said. Morrison said this was “one of the wildest stories we’ve covered in a while” and was full of interesting characters. He said that Serafini wanted him to believe that he was wronged by the jury.Watch the full "Dateline" special Friday at 9 p.m. on KCRA 3. See a preview below.
